messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

For the first nineteen years of his life, Marco had trusted his hands. As an HVAC technician, he worked with his body every day—lifting compressors, threading refrigerant lines, balancing airflow in crawlspaces where the heat pressed in like a weight. He knew his reflexes, his balance, his strength. That trust ended on a Tuesday afternoon in July, on a residential job in a neighborhood of narrow streets and old trees. Marco had been replacing a condenser unit behind a house when a father and his young son came out to the backyard to play catch. Marco didn’t see them until he swung the old unit onto a dolly—a heavy, awkward load—and lost his grip. The unit tipped, and in the seconds it took Marco to realize what was happening, it had already struck the man in the head. The sound was sickening and wet. The boy screamed. Marco’s hands went numb as he knelt beside the man, calling 911, pressing a towel to the wound, but he knew even then that he had not done enough. The man survived, but with lasting neurological damage. Marco has not forgiven himself.

In the months that followed, Marco found himself replaying that moment in fragments—not as a coherent memory, but as a series of sensory intrusions that felt as though they belonged to someone else. He would be driving home from a job and suddenly smell the hot metal of the condenser and the cut grass of that backyard, and he would think, *That isn’t mine. That didn’t happen to me.* But the smell was real, and his heart would slam against his ribs before he could stop it. He had come to believe that his own body was fundamentally unreliable—that his hands, which he had always counted on, could betray him at any moment. Because he could not trust himself, Marco began to avoid anything that might put him in a position to fail again. He stopped taking jobs that involved working near other people. He turned down calls from families with children. He began to avoid dates and anniversaries—the anniversary of the accident, his own birthday, holidays—because each one felt like a trap waiting to spring. He would lie in bed on those days, refusing to move, certain that if he did anything at all, he would cause another disaster.

The more he withdrew, the more his guilt deepened. Marco had begun to feel that the person he had become was unrecognizable—this cautious, fearful man who flinched at his own shadow. He would lie awake at night going over the details of the accident again and again, trying to find the moment where he could have done something different, where he could have been better. But there was no answer, only the certainty that he would never forgive himself for not doing more. And the more he ruminated, the more the memory forced its way into his mind unbidden—the wet sound, the boy’s scream, the smell of grass and blood—and each time it did, his sense of safety evaporated. He had come to believe that silence was dangerous. If his apartment was too quiet, if the HVAC unit at work hummed at a slightly different pitch, his body would seize up, his palms would sweat, and he would be certain that something terrible was about to happen. He had narrowed his world to a handful of places where he felt marginally safe: his bedroom, his truck, and one corner of the supply warehouse where no one ever went. Anywhere else, he felt exposed.

Marco’s supervisor noticed that he was refusing jobs, and after three months, he was moved to part-time. His mother called more often, but Marco stopped answering. He knew that his avoidance was making things worse—that he was shrinking his life down to almost nothing—but he could not see another way. What finally brought him to seek help was a morning in late October, when he woke up in his bedroom and realized he could not remember the last time he had spoken to anyone face to face. He was twenty-two years old, and he was afraid of everything. He was afraid that the therapist would tell him he was beyond help, but he was more afraid of staying the same.
